Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We present mid-infrared (10.4 \micron, 11.7 \micron, and 18.3 \micron) imaging intended to locate and characterize the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. We detect and confirm the protostellar status for the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II. The mid-infrared luminosity for CB54YC1-II was found to be $L_{midir} \approx 8 L_\sun$, and we estimate a central source mass of $M_* \approx 0.8 M_\sun$ (for a mass accretion rate of ${\dot M}=10^{-6} M_\sun yr^{-1}$). CB54 harbors another near-infrared source (CB54YC1-I), which was not detected by our observations. The non-detection is consistent with CB54YC1-I being a highly extinguished embedded young A or B star or a background G or F giant. An alternative explanation for CB54YC1-I is that the source is an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, and the near-infrared detections are not of the central protostar, but of light scattered by the accretion disk into our line of sight. In addition, we have discovered three new mid-infrared sources, which are spatially coincident with the previously known dense core in CB54. The source temperatures ($\sim100$K) and association of the mid-infrared sources with the dense core suggests that these mid-infrared objects may be embedded class 0 protostars.

outputs.L1:
We present mid-infrared imaging at 10.4 \micron, 11.7 \micron, and 18.3 \micron\ aimed at locating and characterizing the suspected protostellar components within the Bok globule CB54. We detect the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II and confirm its protostellar nature. Its mid-infrared luminosity is found to be $L_{midir} \approx 8 L_\sun$, and we estimate a central source mass of $M_* \approx 0.8 M_\sun$, assuming a mass accretion rate of ${\dot M}=10^{-6} M_\sun yr^{-1}$.  

CB54 also harbors another near-infrared source, CB54YC1-I, which was not detected in our observations. This non-detection is consistent with CB54YC1-I being either a highly extinguished, embedded young A or B star, or a background G or F giant. Alternatively, CB54YC1-I may be an embedded protostar viewed at an extremely high inclination angle, such that the near-infrared detections trace not the central protostar itself, but rather light scattered by the accretion disk into our line of sight.  

In addition, we have discovered three new mid-infrared sources that are spatially coincident with the previously known dense core in CB54. Their source temperatures ($\sim100$ K), together with their association with the dense core, suggest that these mid-infrared objects may be embedded Class 0 protostars.
outputs.L2:
We report mid-infrared observations at 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 microns aimed at identifying and studying the candidate protostellar objects in the Bok globule CB54. Our data reveal the near-infrared source CB54YC1-II and verify that it is protostellar in nature. For CB54YC1-II, we derive a mid-infrared luminosity of approximately \(L_{\rm midir} \approx 8\,L_\odot\), and, assuming an accretion rate of \(\dot{M}=10^{-6}\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}\), we estimate the mass of the central object to be about \(M_* \approx 0.8\,M_\odot\).

CB54 also contains a second near-infrared source, CB54YC1-I, but this object was not seen in our mid-infrared images. Its absence from the detections is compatible with it being either a deeply obscured embedded young A- or B-type star, or alternatively a background G- or F-type giant. Another possibility is that CB54YC1-I is an embedded protostar observed nearly edge-on, so that the near-infrared emission detected from it does not come directly from the central protostar but instead consists of radiation scattered into our viewing direction by its accretion disk.

We also identify three previously unknown mid-infrared sources. These objects lie in the same region as the already recognized dense core in CB54. Their inferred temperatures, around \(\sim 100\) K, together with their positional association with the dense core, indicate that they may be embedded Class 0 protostars.
outputs.L3:
Mid-infrared imaging at wavelengths of 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 microns was used to investigate the Bok globule CB54, with the goal of identifying and characterizing suspected protostellar objects embedded within its dense core. These observations are particularly valuable because mid-infrared emission can reveal young stellar objects that are obscured at optical and near-infrared wavelengths by surrounding dust.

One of the main near-infrared sources in the region, CB54YC1-II, was detected in the mid-infrared data. This detection confirms that CB54YC1-II is a protostar rather than a more evolved or unrelated background object. Its mid-infrared luminosity is estimated to be approximately 8 times the luminosity of the Sun, and the inferred mass of its central object is about 0.8 solar masses. These properties are consistent with a young, still-forming star embedded in the globule.

In contrast, the nearby near-infrared source CB54YC1-I was not detected at the observed mid-infrared wavelengths. This non-detection supports earlier interpretations that CB54YC1-I may be either a highly extinguished, embedded young A- or B-type star, or a background G- or F-type giant seen through the molecular cloud. In either case, the absence of detectable mid-infrared emission suggests that it does not have the same clear protostellar signature seen in CB54YC1-II.

However, another possibility remains: CB54YC1-I could be an embedded protostar viewed nearly edge-on, at a very high inclination angle. In such a geometry, direct infrared radiation from the central source would be heavily blocked by the circumstellar disk and envelope, while the observed near-infrared emission could be dominated by scattered light escaping along the disk or outflow cavities. This scenario would explain why the object appears in the near-infrared but is not detected in the mid-infrared observations.

In addition to studying the previously known near-infrared sources, the mid-infrared observations revealed three new sources within the dense core of CB54. Their locations deep inside the globule and their inferred low temperatures suggest that they may be very young, deeply embedded class 0 protostars. If confirmed, these objects would represent some of the earliest stages of star formation in CB54, indicating that the globule contains multiple sites of ongoing protostellar activity.
outputs.L4:
Mid-infrared observations of the Bok globule CB54 were carried out at wavelengths of 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 microns in order to identify and characterize candidate protostellar objects embedded in the cloud. These wavelengths are well suited for detecting warm dust emission associated with young stellar objects, especially sources still surrounded by dense circumstellar envelopes. The study focused on previously suspected protostellar candidates in CB54, particularly the objects known as CB54YC1-I and CB54YC1-II, and also searched for additional compact mid-infrared sources within dense cores of the globule.

The observations clearly detect CB54YC1-II and confirm that it is a protostellar source. Its mid-infrared emission, together with existing longer-wavelength data, is consistent with a young embedded object of approximately 8 solar luminosities. Modeling of the source suggests that it contains a central object with an estimated mass of about 0.8 solar masses. These properties indicate that CB54YC1-II is likely an intermediate stage young stellar object still surrounded by significant dust and gas.

In contrast, CB54YC1-I was not detected in the mid-infrared images. This non-detection leaves its nature uncertain. It may be too deeply embedded, too cold, or intrinsically too faint to be detected at the observed wavelengths, or it may not be a protostar at all. Additional observations at far-infrared, submillimeter, or millimeter wavelengths would be needed to determine whether CB54YC1-I contains an embedded source.

The imaging also revealed three previously unidentified mid-infrared sources located within dense cores of CB54. Their association with dense material suggests that they may be very young embedded protostars, possibly class 0 objects. If confirmed, these sources would represent some of the earliest stages of star formation in the globule. Overall, the mid-infrared observations show that CB54 is an active site of low-mass star formation, containing at least one confirmed protostar and several additional candidate embedded objects requiring further study.
outputs.L5:
**Bok, The**

“Bok” is a word with rich meaning. In several Scandinavian languages, *bok* means “book,” a symbol of knowledge, imagination, and memory. A book can open doors to distant places, introduce new ideas, and preserve stories for future generations. Whether it is a novel, a history text, or a personal journal, a bok has the power to connect people across time and culture.

The word *bok* can also refer to the beech tree in some languages, a tree long associated with wisdom and writing. In ancient times, people carved symbols into wood, and the connection between trees and books remains strong today through paper, libraries, and storytelling.

In this sense, “Bok, The” can be understood as a celebration of both nature and knowledge: the tree that gives material, and the book that gives meaning. It reminds us that learning grows like a forest—slowly, deeply, and beautifully.

counterfactuals.output: We present mid-infrared imaging observations of the Bok globule CB54 obtained at 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 μm, aimed at identifying and characterizing embedded young stellar objects associated with ongoing star formation in the core. The images reveal compact infrared emission coincident with the previously known embedded source population, demonstrating that several objects in CB54 are detectable at wavelengths sensitive to warm circumstellar dust. The 10.4 and 11.7 μm data trace emission from heated inner envelope or disk material, while the 18.3 μm observations provide evidence for cooler dust components associated with more deeply embedded protostellar sources. The measured mid-infrared fluxes, together with existing near-infrared and far-infrared constraints, indicate that the brightest sources are likely low- to intermediate-mass protostars rather than externally heated dust condensations. Source morphology and wavelength-dependent brightness variations suggest differing evolutionary stages and circumstellar environments within the globule. These results support the interpretation of CB54 as an active site of clustered, embedded star formation and demonstrate the utility of mid-infrared imaging for resolving protostellar candidates in dense Bok globules.

counterfactuals.output: In summary, our 10.4, 11.7, and 18.3 μm imaging of the Bok globule CB54 provides a sensitive mid-infrared view of its embedded young stellar population and associated warm dust emission. The data reveal a concentration of mid-infrared sources coincident with the dense core, consistent with a small cluster of young stellar objects at different evolutionary stages. The rising mid-infrared continua and enhanced 18.3 μm emission of the reddest objects indicate substantial circumstellar material, identifying them as the most deeply embedded protostellar candidates, while comparatively bluer sources are consistent with more evolved pre-main-sequence stars with disks. Extended emission at mid-infrared wavelengths traces heated dust in the immediate environment of the young sources, suggesting that local radiative feedback is already shaping the structure of the globule on small spatial scales. Together, these observations confirm CB54 as an active site of low- to intermediate-mass star formation and demonstrate the utility of narrow-band mid-infrared imaging for separating embedded protostars, disk-bearing young stars, and diffuse dust emission in compact molecular cloud cores. Further longer-wavelength photometry and spectroscopy will be required to constrain the bolometric luminosities, envelope masses, and evolutionary status of the individual sources more robustly.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an astrophysics abstract reporting mid-infrared detections in CB54: confirmation of CB54YC1-II as a protostar, non-detection scenarios for CB54YC1-I, and discovery of three embedded sources near the dense core.
counterfactuals.output:
We present mid-infrared observations of the Bok globule CB54 aimed at identifying the embedded young stellar population associated with its dense molecular core. The previously proposed source CB54YC1-II is clearly detected at mid-infrared wavelengths and exhibits rising infrared emission consistent with a deeply embedded young stellar object. Its spectral energy distribution and location relative to the dense gas confirm CB54YC1-II as a bona fide protostar rather than a background contaminant or externally heated condensation.

In contrast, no secure mid-infrared counterpart is detected at the reported position of CB54YC1-I. This non-detection admits several possibilities: CB54YC1-I may be an extremely cold, very low luminosity object whose emission peaks at far-infrared or submillimetre wavelengths; it may be a starless or prestellar core with no internal source; or the earlier identification may have been affected by positional uncertainty, confusion, or extended dust emission. Additional high-resolution far-infrared/submillimetre imaging and molecular-line data are required to distinguish among these scenarios.

Our observations also reveal three previously unreported mid-infrared sources projected close to the dense core. Their red colours, compact morphologies, and association with the high-extinction region indicate that they are likely embedded young stellar objects rather than unrelated field stars. The discovery of these sources suggests that CB54 hosts a small, clustered episode of low-mass star formation, with multiple protostellar or pre-main-sequence objects forming within the same dense globule. These results demonstrate the importance of mid-infrared imaging for completing the census of embedded sources in isolated star-forming cores and provide new constraints on the evolutionary state and star-formation activity of CB54.
